title: Classical Classification and Clustering
subtitle: Apply and tune logistic regression, k-NN, SVMs, decision trees and ensembles, then find structure in unlabelled data with k-means and PCA, all in scikit-learn.
outcomes: Train and tune logistic regression and k-NN classifiers, and compare classifiers with ROC AUC and cross-validation
Apply support vector machines with linear, polynomial and RBF kernels, tuning C and gamma
Build, prune and read decision trees, and beat them with random forests and gradient boosting
Cluster unlabelled data with k-means, choosing K with the elbow method and silhouette scores
Reduce dimensions with PCA to compress data, visualise it and speed up models
Build an end-to-end pipeline that selects the best classifier by cross-validation
prerequisites: Machine Learning Foundations with Python, or Foundations of Machine Learning (Vietnamese and English): train/test splits, fitting scikit-learn models and basic metrics. Comfortable Python with pandas and NumPy. Machine Learning from Scratch is a good companion: it builds several of these algorithms by hand. Install Python 3 with NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib and JupyterLab; every dataset ships with scikit-learn or the labs.
description:
This course is a practical tour of the classical algorithms that still solve most tabular problems, each applied, tuned and understood in scikit-learn. You start with logistic regression, reading its coefficients as odds ratios and controlling it with C and L1 or L2 penalties, and k-nearest neighbours, with its distance metrics, k and weights, and compare classifiers properly with ROC curves, AUC and shared cross-validation folds. Then come support vector machines: maximum margins, support vectors, the kernel trick, the tuning of C and gamma, and calibrated probabilities. Decision trees follow, with information gain and pruning, and then the ensembles that fix their weaknesses: bagging, random forests with out-of-bag scores and permutation importance, gradient boosting, voting and stacking.

The last two modules turn to unlabelled data. You cluster with k-means, choose K with the elbow method and silhouette scores, and learn where DBSCAN or hierarchical clustering fit better; then you reduce dimensions with PCA, choosing components by explained variance, compressing data and mapping it in two dimensions beside t-SNE. Every lesson has a JupyterLab walkthrough with real outputs, and every module a lab on data such as scikit-learn's wine and digits sets and a made-up football dataset, where clustering rediscovers playing styles. The capstone is an end-to-end pipeline that compares classifier families by cross-validation and selects the best one.

modules.title: Logistic Regression & KNN
modules.summary: Two classic classifiers from opposite traditions: logistic regression, which turns a weighted sum into a probability, and k-nearest neighbours, which votes among similar examples. Tune both, read what they learned, and compare them fairly with ROC AUC.

lessons.title: Logistic regression: probabilities, log-odds and regularisation
objectives: Explain how the sigmoid turns a linear score into a probability
Read coefficients as changes in log-odds and odds ratios
Control model complexity with C and choose between L2 and L1 penalties
key_points: Logistic regression outputs probabilities: the sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) maps the linear score z = w · x + b to a value between 0 and 1. Despite its name it is a classifier.

The score is the log-odds, log(p / (1 − p)) = w · x + b, so a coefficient w_j is the change in log-odds when x_j rises by one unit, and e^(w_j) multiplies the odds; on standardised features, the unit is one standard deviation.

scikit-learn regularises by default: C (1.0 unless set) is the inverse of the penalty's strength, so a smaller C means smaller weights and a simpler model. On the standardised wine data the largest coefficient is 0.25 at C=0.01, 1.14 at C=1 and 3.41 at C=100.

L2 shrinks every coefficient towards zero; L1 sets some exactly to zero, a form of feature selection. In scikit-learn 1.8 and later choose L1 with l1_ratio=1 (earlier versions: penalty='l1') and a solver that supports it, such as 'saga'.

With more than two classes, LogisticRegression's default lbfgs solver fits one multinomial (softmax) model: one coefficient vector per class, so coef_ has shape (3, 13) for the wine data, and probabilities that sum to 1.
Standardise the features in a pipeline, so that the penalty treats them equally and the solver converges; raise max_iter if scikit-learn warns that it didn't.

lessons.title: k-nearest neighbours: distance metrics, k and weights
objectives: Choose a distance metric and vote weighting for k-NN
Tune k with cross-validation inside a pipeline
Explain how irrelevant features hurt k-NN
key_points: k-NN classifies a sample by a vote of its k nearest training samples. scikit-learn's default metric is Minkowski with p=2, the Euclidean distance; p=1 gives the Manhattan distance, the sum of absolute differences (5.0 against 7 between (0, 0) and (3, 4)).
weights='distance' gives nearer neighbours bigger votes, in proportion to 1/distance, which makes a large k less likely to wash out a local pattern.

k is a hyperparameter: small k gives low bias and high variance, large k the reverse. Tune it with cross-validation together with the metric and the weights, with the scaler inside the pipeline so that each fold is scaled on its own training part.
Every feature counts in the distance, so irrelevant features add noise: on the wine data, 5-fold accuracy with k=15 is 0.967, and adding 50 columns of random noise drops it to 0.916.
Prediction compares each query with the training set, so k-NN suits small to medium data with a modest number of meaningful features; algorithm='auto' picks a KD-tree, a ball tree or brute force.

lessons.title: Comparing classifiers: ROC curves and AUC
objectives: Read a ROC curve and its AUC
Choose between ROC AUC, average precision and accuracy
Compare models fairly on the same cross-validation folds
key_points: A ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate as the decision threshold moves from high to low, showing every threshold's trade-off at once.
AUC, the area under the ROC curve, is the probability that a random positive is scored higher than a random negative: 0.5 is chance and 1.0 a perfect ranking, whatever threshold is used later.
AUC needs scores, not labels: pass predict_proba(X)[:, 1] or decision_function(X). For more than two classes, roc_auc_score(y, proba, multi_class='ovr') averages the one-against-the-rest AUCs.
Accuracy hides weak models when classes are imbalanced: with 10% positives, models scoring 0.907 and 0.912 accuracy, barely above always saying no, can differ a lot in ROC AUC (0.733 and 0.892).
With rare positives, the precision-recall curve and its summary, average precision, show the difference more clearly than ROC, because the many true negatives keep the false positive rate small.
Compare models on the same folds with the same metric (a StratifiedKFold with shuffle=True and a random_state), report the mean and the spread, and keep the test set for the final model.

modules.title: Support Vector Machines
modules.summary: Separate classes with the widest possible margin, let a few support vectors define the boundary, and bend it with kernels: tune C and gamma, and turn SVM scores into calibrated probabilities.

lessons.title: Maximum margins and support vectors
objectives: Explain the margin and the support vectors of a linear SVM
Describe how C trades margin width against training errors
key_points: A linear SVM separates two classes with the hyperplane w · x + b = 0 that has the widest margin, the gap to the nearest training points of each class; the margin's width is 2 / ‖w‖.

The support vectors are the training points on or inside the margin. They alone define the boundary: moving any other point, without crossing the margin, changes nothing. SVC exposes them as support_vectors_ and their count per class as n_support_.

A soft margin lets some points sit inside the margin or on the wrong side, at a cost set by C: small C gives a wide margin with many support vectors (more regularisation), large C a narrow margin that fits the training points harder.

The soft-margin SVM minimises the hinge loss, max(0, 1 − y · f(x)) with labels ±1, plus a penalty on ‖w‖²: points beyond the margin on the right side cost nothing, so only the support vectors shape the solution.
SVMs are distance-based, so standardise the features. For large data, LinearSVC fits a linear SVM much faster than SVC(kernel='linear').

print(svm.coef_.round(3), svm.intercept_.round(3), round(2 / np.linalg.norm(svm.coef_), 3))

lessons.title: The kernel trick
objectives: Explain how kernels let a linear method draw curved boundaries
Describe the linear, polynomial and RBF kernels and the effect of gamma
key_points: Classes that no straight line separates can become separable after adding features, such as x₁² + x₂² for two rings; the kernel trick computes the dot products in that bigger space without ever building its features.
A kernel k(x, x′) measures similarity. Linear: x · x′. Polynomial: (γ x · x′ + coef0)^degree. RBF (Gaussian): exp(−γ ‖x − x′‖²), SVC's default, which can draw very flexible boundaries.

gamma sets how far one training point's influence reaches with the RBF kernel: small gamma gives smooth, almost linear boundaries; large gamma gives wiggly boundaries around single points, and overfits. The default, gamma='scale', is 1 / (n_features × X.var()).
The fitted decision function is a weighted sum of kernel similarities to the support vectors, plus b, so prediction slows as the number of support vectors grows.
SVC's fit time grows at least quadratically with the number of samples, which makes it impractical beyond tens of thousands of samples; LinearSVC or SGDClassifier scale much further.

lessons.title: Tuning C and gamma, and getting probabilities
objectives: Tune C and gamma together with cross-validation
Get calibrated probabilities from an SVM
Handle multiclass and imbalanced problems with SVC
key_points: C and gamma interact, so tune them together on log-spaced grids, such as 0.1 to 100 for C and 0.01 to 10 for gamma, with cross-validation and the scaler inside the pipeline.
SVC's decision_function returns signed distances from the boundary, not probabilities; their sign gives the class.

For probabilities, wrap the model in CalibratedClassifierCV(SVC(), ensemble=False), which learns a mapping from scores to probabilities with internal cross-validation. SVC(probability=True) is deprecated from scikit-learn 1.9 in its favour.
With more than two classes SVC trains one classifier per pair of classes (one-vs-one) and combines their votes; decision_function_shape='ovr', the default, reports one score per class.
class_weight='balanced' raises the penalty for errors on rarer classes, in inverse proportion to their frequency: a simple first fix for imbalanced data.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC

modules.summary: Grow interpretable trees and prune them, then combine many trees: bagging and random forests to reduce variance, gradient boosting to reduce bias, and voting and stacking to mix different models.

lessons.title: Decision trees: information gain and pruning
objectives: Explain how a tree chooses its splits
Prune a tree with depth limits and cost-complexity pruning
key_points: A tree splits the data with yes/no questions about one feature at a time, choosing each split to maximise the information gain: the fall in impurity, measured by Gini (scikit-learn's default) or entropy.

Grown fully, a tree fits its training data perfectly and overfits. Pre-pruning limits its growth (max_depth, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes); post-pruning cuts it back with cost-complexity pruning, set by ccp_alpha.

cost_complexity_pruning_path lists the alphas at which subtrees are pruned away; choose ccp_alpha by cross-validation. On the wine data, alpha 0.011 cuts the tree from 12 leaves to 8 with no loss in cross-validated accuracy.
Trees need no scaling, capture interactions and non-linear effects, and are easy to read with export_text or plot_tree; but they are unstable, and their boundaries are made of axis-aligned steps.

A smooth, round boundary is hard for one tree: on make_hastie_10_2, where the class depends on the distance from the centre, even a pruned tree reaches only about 0.75 test accuracy. That is where ensembles come in.

lessons.title: Random forests: bagging and random features
objectives: Explain how bagging and random feature choice reduce variance
Use out-of-bag scores and permutation importance
key_points: Ensembles combine several models into a better one. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains each model on a bootstrap sample, rows drawn with replacement, and averages their votes, which reduces variance.

A random forest bags deep trees and, at every split, considers only a random subset of the features (max_features='sqrt' by default for classifiers), which makes the trees less alike, so averaging helps more.
A bootstrap sample contains about 63% of the distinct rows, so each tree leaves out about a third; oob_score=True scores every row with the trees that didn't see it, a free estimate of test accuracy.
More trees don't make a forest overfit; they cost time, and the score levels off, as between 50 and 200 trees in the lab.

feature_importances_ is impurity-based: computed on training data and biased towards features with many distinct values. permutation_importance on held-out data, which measures how much the score drops when one feature is shuffled, is more trustworthy.

lessons.title: Boosting, voting and stacking
objectives: Explain how gradient boosting builds an ensemble step by step
Combine different models by voting and stacking
key_points: Boosting builds models one after another, each correcting the ones before: gradient boosting fits every new small tree to the gradient of the loss (for squared error, the residuals) and adds it, scaled by the learning rate.

The learning rate and the number of trees trade off: smaller steps need more trees and usually generalise better. On make_hastie_10_2, stumps boosted with a learning rate of 0.5 go from 0.532 test accuracy after 1 tree to 0.914 after 200.

HistGradientBoostingClassifier bins each feature into at most 255 bins, which makes it fast on large data; it handles missing values natively and turns early stopping on automatically for more than 10,000 samples.

Voting averages different models' predictions, hard votes or probabilities (voting='soft'); stacking trains a final model on their cross-validated predictions. Both help most when the models make different mistakes.

Bagging and forests mainly reduce variance, averaging deep, noisy trees; boosting mainly reduces bias, adding up shallow, weak ones. Boosting is often the strongest choice for tabular data, but needs more tuning.

modules.title: K-Means Clustering
modules.summary: Discover groups in unlabelled data with centroid-based clustering: run k-means well, choose K with the elbow method and silhouette scores, profile the clusters, and know when another method fits better.

lessons.title: How k-means works, and how to use it well
objectives: Run k-means with sensible initialisation and scaling
Profile clusters in the original units
key_points: K-Means partitions data into K clusters by minimising the inertia, the sum of squared distances from points to their cluster's centroid, alternating two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points.

K must be chosen beforehand, and the result depends on the starting centroids: k-means++ (the default) spreads them out, n_init runs several starts and keeps the lowest inertia, and random_state makes the result repeatable.

Standardise first: unscaled, the feature with the largest spread dominates the distances. In the player data that is passes per 90 minutes (standard deviation 17.0, against about 1 for the others), and unscaled clusters mostly sort players by passes.

A fitted KMeans has labels_, cluster_centers_ (in the scaled space: inverse_transform them to read them in the original units), inertia_, and predict, which assigns new samples to the nearest centroid.
Cluster numbers are arbitrary. Describe each cluster by its centre and size and give it a name a person can check, such as 'high tackles and aerial duels: defenders'.

lessons.title: Choosing K: the elbow and the silhouette
objectives: Use the elbow method and silhouette scores to choose K
Compare a clustering with known groups using the adjusted Rand index
key_points: Inertia always falls as K grows, reaching 0 when every point is its own cluster, so its minimum can't choose K. The elbow method plots inertia against K and looks for the bend after which extra clusters gain little.

A sample's silhouette is (b − a) / max(a, b), where a is its mean distance to its own cluster and b to the nearest other cluster: near 1 it sits well inside its cluster, near 0 on a border, and below 0 probably in the wrong one.

silhouette_score averages it over all samples (it needs K ≥ 2), and higher is better. The two methods can disagree: on three blobs where two sit close together, the silhouette prefers K = 2 while the elbow points at 3.
Use domain sense as well: clusters must be useful to someone, and stable across random starts and samples of the data.
When true groups are known for some data, the adjusted Rand index compares a clustering with them: 1 means the same groups (whatever their numbers), and about 0 means no better than random.

lessons.title: When k-means fails, and alternatives
objectives: Recognise data that k-means can't cluster well
Choose DBSCAN or hierarchical clustering instead
key_points: K-Means assumes compact, roughly round clusters of similar size and spread, because every point goes to its nearest centroid: long, curved, nested or very unequal clusters break it.
Every point is forced into some cluster, and outliers pull centroids towards themselves.
DBSCAN groups points that lie in dense regions, finds clusters of any shape and labels points in sparse regions as noise (−1); it needs eps, the neighbourhood radius, and min_samples instead of K.

Agglomerative (hierarchical) clustering merges the closest clusters step by step; the linkage, such as ward, average, complete or single, defines 'closest', and a dendrogram shows the order of the merges.
Gaussian mixture models (GaussianMixture) allow elliptical clusters and give each point a probability of belonging to each cluster instead of a hard label.

modules.title: PCA & Dimensionality Reduction
modules.summary: Reduce many features to a few with principal component analysis: see what the components are, choose how many to keep, compress and reconstruct data, speed up models, and map high-dimensional data in two dimensions.

lessons.title: What PCA finds
objectives: Explain principal components as orthogonal directions of maximum variance
Read loadings and explained variance
Decide when to standardise before PCA
key_points: Principal component analysis (PCA) finds orthogonal axes, the principal components, ordered by how much of the data's variance each captures; projecting onto the first few keeps as much of the spread as any linear projection can.
Each component is a linear combination of the original features. Its weights, the loadings, are in components_, and explained_variance_ratio_ gives each component's share of the total variance.

PCA centres the data and works from its covariance matrix: the components are the matrix's eigenvectors and explained_variance_ its eigenvalues; scikit-learn computes them with the singular value decomposition.
Standardise first when features have different units, or the feature with the largest variance takes over the first component: on the raw player data PC1 is almost exactly passes (loading 1.00).
PCA is unsupervised and linear: it ignores the labels, can miss curved structure, and a component's sign is arbitrary.
